title: Inside Out
speaker: Josh Wyatt
card_summary: A chronological study outline of the message’s call to inward honesty, confession, cleansing, forgiveness, and a renewed heart.
section_intro: The outline begins with communion, follows the sermon’s verse-by-verse movements through Psalm 51:6–9, and preserves the closing application and prayer. Scripture tags jump to the verified reference table.

This outline quotes only brief identifying phrases and does not reproduce the full transcript or full NIV text.

ledger_intro: One row is provided for each confirmed spoken Scripture unit or range. Short phrases identify the use without reproducing the full biblical text. Bible links open the NIV.
ledger_caption: 37 confirmed Scripture units, in sermon order

movements.heading: The Lord’s table calls believers to true self-examination
bullets: Josh opens from Crossroads’ weekly practice of communion and says no sermon has ministered to him as consistently as the Lord’s table.
Holding the signs of Christ’s body and blood leaves nowhere to hide and demands true confession before communion.

children.heading: Communion exposes the worshiper
bullets: The Lord’s table confronts the communicant with Christ’s sacrifice and requires confession rather than concealment.

children.heading: Paul tells Christians to examine themselves
bullets: Josh reads Paul’s warning that believers should examine themselves before eating and drinking, discern Christ’s body, and avoid bringing judgment on themselves.
He stresses that Christians—not merely unbelievers—are under the microscope in the passage and may approach the meal in an unworthy manner.

children.heading: Unworthy and worthy approaches to communion
bullets: Going through the motions, treating the ceremony itself as saving, harboring bitterness, unforgiveness, hatred, criticism, or refusing repentance are presented as unworthy approaches.
The worthy approach is worshipful attention to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and genuine love for God and fellow believers; otherwise, Josh says, let the meal pass.
Celebrating the cross that removed sin while carrying unconfessed sin is hypocrisy, and Paul’s warning is described as fatherly discipline.

children.heading: Table manners and the call to wash before the table
bullets: A mother correcting ordinary table manners illustrates that every table has a right and wrong approach.
The familiar question “Did you wash your hands?” becomes the bridge from Paul’s command to examine oneself to walking through Psalm 51.

children.heading: Why preaching helps the preacher and the church
bullets: Preaching first forces Josh to examine his own wounds before asking the congregation to examine theirs; unlike the perfect Jesus, he must address his own imperfections before helping others.
He also values preaching because the Spirit can use any text, illustration, or statement in an unexpected listener’s life.
Two recent testimonies of heart and life change reinforce the value of gathering in person rather than forsaking congregational life.

children.heading: The series slows down at Psalm 51:6
bullets: After a thirteen-week passage through Hebrews, this series has six weeks for nineteen verses.
The riding-mower turtle and rabbit settings illustrate the deliberate “turtle mode” pace before verse 6 is read.

movements.heading: God delights in truth within, not surface cleanliness
bullets: Psalm 51:6 reveals the contrast between God’s delight in inward truth and David’s life of falsehood.
The sermon moves from external washing to the heart as the source of defilement and applies that distinction to parenting.

children.heading: Psalm 51:6 states God’s inward desire
bullets: Josh reads that God delights in truth in the inward being and teaches wisdom in the secret heart.
He refuses to treat the verse as a mere transition and gives it sustained attention.

children.heading: David moves from confession to diagnosis
bullets: Verses 1–5 are recapped as David’s confession after Nathan confronted his adultery and murder: David knows his transgression, admits sin against God, and acknowledges sin from conception.
David sees that God desires truth while he has been living a lie; the problem is not that facts leaked but that truth within him stopped ruling.
Rather than asking only how to repair events, David keeps digging and asks what has gone wrong in him that he would act this way.

children.heading: Jesus locates defilement in the heart
bullets: In Matthew 15, Pharisees object to the disciples eating without ceremonial washing, but Jesus turns attention from hands to hearts.

Josh quotes Jesus that what enters the mouth passes through the body, whereas evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander come from the heart and defile a person.
A story about Josh’s young son using the passage to resist washing his hands shows the danger of detaching a text from its context.

children.heading: Parents must watch what comes out of children’s hearts
bullets: Josh addresses mothers, grandmothers, aunts, and others with influence over children, affirming their extraordinary influence over the next generation.
Careful monitoring of food, sugar, allergies, snacks, water, and vitamins is contrasted with neglect of anger, entitlement, disrespect, dishonesty, cruelty, and foolishness.
The church supports parents, but Josh assigns parents responsibility for training children in the Lord.
The goal is not merely public behavior, achievement, scholarships, or a career; a well-mannered, successful child without a new heart may still reject Jesus.

children.heading: Lois and Eunice model sincere faith and Scripture in the home
bullets: Paul’s words about Timothy are used to show that sincere faith lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice before it was evident in his ministry.
Timothy knew the sacred Scriptures from childhood, and those Scriptures could make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ.
Lois and Eunice taught more than worldly success; they taught truth that led Timothy to Jesus.

children.heading: Parents are asked to examine the sincerity children see
bullets: Mothers and grandmothers are asked whether children see sincere rather than flawless faith in them.

Concrete tests include confessing wrongs, owning mistakes, opening Scripture, seeking wisdom, praying together, and praying for grace, forgiveness, and wisdom rather than only safety, success, grades, and food.
They are asked whether loving Jesus visibly matters more than teams, scholarships, or an impressive life.
The answer is not to make Bible reading one more item on a chore chart.

children.heading: The problem is beneath behavior, at the root
bullets: Rules alone cannot repair what is wrong because the problem lies below the surface.
David does not merely ask for rotten fruit to be removed; he asks God to address the root producing it.
What repeatedly comes out reveals what lives within, and God seeks inward truth and secret-heart wisdom rather than an externally clean appearance.

children.heading: God’s commands are good, but Psalm 51 names his delight
bullets: Josh contrasts inward truth with rule-keeping, appearance management, behavior control, prohibitions, reputation protection, and avoidance of visible consequences.
He affirms that God’s commands are good and glorious, while insisting that believers ask not only what God forbids but what he delights in.
Psalm 51 answers that God delights in truth.

movements.heading: David’s false world exposes the need for inward truth
bullets: David’s failure is traced beyond lust to the false narrative built to hide it.
The same inward-truth demand is applied to hypocrisy, image management, secondhand faith, and personal confession.

children.heading: Psalm 15 joins dwelling with God to truth from the heart
bullets: Josh quotes David’s question about who may dwell in God’s sanctuary and the answer that such people speak truth from their hearts.

children.heading: Lust was the trailer; falsehood was the movie
bullets: The audience chooses whether lust or falsehood best describes David’s sin with Bathsheba.
Josh says lust initiated the episode, but falsehood became the larger story, and he assigns 2 Samuel 11 as homework.
David sees Bathsheba, takes her, learns she is pregnant, and begins constructing a narrative to conceal the truth.

children.heading: Narrative-building recruits others and should be resisted
bullets: A side application warns that quickly building a narrative about another person requires talking to someone else about that person.
Proverbs says the first case sounds right until it is examined by another; Josh counsels pausing, praying, and waiting rather than joining the narrative.
Quick narrative-building is associated with something being covered.

children.heading: David’s cover-up becomes murder and public spin
bullets: David brings Uriah home to sleep with Bathsheba, gets him drunk when he refuses, and finally sends him back carrying the order that brings his death.
After Uriah dies, David takes Bathsheba as his wife, allowing the public story to look like a gracious king caring for a fallen soldier’s widow.
The public spin looks noble, but the deed displeases the Lord; David lives inside the manufactured false world for about a year.

children.heading: God seeks actual inward truth, not truth-telling as performance
bullets: God is not after advantageous truth-telling alone but truth in the inward parts: the unseen and unsaid realities.
A polished bucket cannot fix a poisoned well, and religious appearance cannot cover inward corruption before God.
The demand is for true repentance and actual faith, not their shadow, picture, sound, or vocabulary.
Hypocrisy may deceive a church, family, friends, or even the hypocrite, but it never deceives God.

children.heading: Image management fragments the self
bullets: Modern image management produces public, work, church, social, social-media, and marriage selves alongside a hidden raw self.
Josh identifies that hidden self as the place where God wants to begin working.
“Wisdom in the secret heart” means truth must reach the being, not remain only in the brain.

children.heading: Knowing doctrine is not the same as being conquered by truth
bullets: A person may know doctrines of grace without being conquered by grace, and accurate theology may coexist with accusation and harshness.
One may explain the cross without kneeling before it or defend Christ’s character without delighting in him.
Doctrine is precious because it identifies God truly, but it is not a hiding place; knowing the language of repentance is useless without repenting.

children.heading: Secondhand Christianity cannot save
bullets: People may borrow testimonies, songs, phrases, joys, and sorrows from other Christians and sound Christian without personally knowing those realities.
Words and Christian-sounding language do not save or substitute for nearness to Christ.
Josh calls for personally confessing sin, fleeing to Christ’s cleansing blood, loving Jesus, talking and walking with him, and being known by him.

children.heading: The test is whether truth has reached and changed the heart
bullets: The demons’ knowledge and trembling show that mere factual recognition is not enough.
Josh asks whether truth has reached the inward parts, humbled the hearer, changed anything, and made Jesus precious.
Friends, family, a pastor, oneself may be fooled; God searches the heart and is not interested in the successfully presented version of a person.

children.heading: A testimony displays grace through confessed ugliness
bullets: A believer’s recent testimony encouraged Josh because public honesty about Josh’s own lies, pride, selfishness, and addictions had helped another believer return to the Lord.
He praises God for taking truths people hide and bury, cleansing them, and making their lives public displays of grace.
Amazing grace means freedom to stop pretending, put down the mask, and stop defending an image because God already knows everything and sent his Son to save.

children.heading: God enters the place where the mask is managed
bullets: Hearers are asked where they perform, manage, polish, or say “I’m fine” when they should admit wretchedness.
David’s confidence is that God enters the hidden place and works exactly where humanity’s fall has corrupted it.
The transition is made from teaching right and wrong to God teaching wisdom.

movements.heading: Wisdom is truth possessed and lived
bullets: Truth names reality; wisdom rightly lives according to it.
Scripture written outside a person must be inscribed by the Spirit upon human hearts so believers become living letters.

children.heading: Truth and wisdom are distinguished
bullets: Knowing what is right does not guarantee doing it; both truth and wisdom are needed.
Truth is defined as knowledge of reality, while wisdom is rightly living according to that truth.

children.heading: Wisdom puts true claims into action
bullets: Truth says sin destroys; wisdom runs from it.
Truth informs people what is real; wisdom navigates that reality.
Truth says the resurrected Christ is enough; wisdom builds a life on him.
Wisdom is summarized as truth in action and truth lived out.

children.heading: Romans names reality; Jesus commands abiding life
bullets: Romans states that sin’s wages are death and God’s gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus.
Jesus’ vine-and-branches saying shows wisdom as abiding, staying with him, speaking to him, and asking from him because apart from him nothing can be done.

children.heading: Truth on a scroll becomes truth written on a person
bullets: Josh contrasts truth written on a scroll for reading with wisdom as God writing truth on a person for others to read.
John’s closing statement that the world could not contain all the books about Jesus’ works is proposed as a picture that may remain open as Christ continues writing his story in changed lives.

children.heading: Believers are letters from Christ written on hearts
bullets: Paul’s words to Corinth identify believers as Christ’s letter, written not with ink but by the living God’s Spirit, not on stone tablets but human hearts.
Truth may be carved in stone, memorized, recited, and defended while the soul remains unchanged.
David knew the commands against adultery, murder, and coveting his neighbor’s wife, but knowledge outside him did not keep him from violating them.

children.heading: David asks that known truth become lived wisdom
bullets: David’s problem was not a failure by God to write truth but David’s failure to live what was written.
Josh voices David’s plea for God to take external truth and inscribe it on his heart until he becomes a living letter of grace.

children.heading: Changed lives become living volumes of Christ’s work
bullets: Every cleansed sinner, straightened heart, and restored life becomes another living declaration of what the Lord has done.
The congregation is invited to stand as testimony that Jesus has changed them and they are not returning to what they were.
The visible response is named as lives washed and cleansed by Christ.

movements.heading: “Purge me with hyssop”: God cleanses from the inside out
bullets: Psalm 51:7 introduces hyssop as a biblical sign of purification and blood.
The sermon traces hyssop from Passover and purification rites to Jesus’ crucifixion, then unfolds David’s confidence that God can make him truly clean.

children.heading: David asks to be purged and washed beyond snow
bullets: Josh reads David’s request to be purged with hyssop and be clean, washed and made whiter than snow.

children.heading: Hyssop serves purification in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers
bullets: In Exodus 12, hyssop carries Passover blood to the doorposts.
In Leviticus 14, the priest uses hyssop in sprinkling the person being cleansed from leprosy.

In Numbers 19, cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet wool are thrown into the red heifer’s fire; the ashes are mixed with fresh water, and hyssop is dipped into the cleansing water to sprinkle a tent, its furnishings, and persons defiled by contact with death.

children.heading: David identifies with captivity, exclusion, disease, and death
bullets: By asking for hyssop, David identifies himself with captives, the outcast leper, and people rendered unclean through disease or death.

children.heading: Hyssop appears at Calvary
bullets: Josh explicitly turns to John 19:29 and reads of wine vinegar on a sponge lifted to Jesus on a hyssop stalk.
He continues through Jesus’ declaration “It is finished,” his bowed head, and the giving up of his spirit.

children.heading: The plant traces cleansing history to the cross
bullets: The congregation is told it stands on holy ground as hyssop is traced from Egypt’s doorposts and the tabernacle to the crucifixion outside Jerusalem.
There the Son of God gives himself to rescue his people from sin and death.
Josh asks the congregation to see and smell the plant and let it preach to their souls in anticipation of a later embodied worship response.

children.heading: The outcast is restored, and David expects appointed purification
bullets: The hearer is asked to imagine an excluded leper rejoining the assembly and singing again, welcomed among God’s people through Jesus.
David is described as confident that God’s appointed provision will finish purification for his people.
His language is not “I might be clean” but “I shall be clean,” trusting God’s power despite his own filth.

children.heading: God’s grace can make cleaner than fresh snow
bullets: Fresh snow is David’s brightest imaginable comparison, yet he asks for a cleansing even whiter than snow.
Snow can cover a filthy field without changing the field beneath it; God does better by working from the inside out.

children.heading: God’s purity is inward and enduring
bullets: Snow gathers dirt and melts under heat, but God can give an enduring purity that survives judgment.
David asks not merely to appear clean but actually to be clean where only God sees.
The requested cleansing reaches memory, motives, imagination, nightmares, and every inward place touched by sin.

children.heading: The gospel removes the stain rather than concealing it
bullets: The blood of Jesus is said to wash away sin rather than merely hide its stain.
Memories, consequences, and scars may remain, but when God cleanses the sinner, the stain does not remain.

children.heading: The accuser points backward; faith points to the cross
bullets: The accuser says “Look at what you’ve done” and calls the person filthy, while faith answers “Look at what the Lord has done.”
The sermon quotes that Jesus’ blood cleanses from all sin and says Jesus names his people friend, brother, sister, and co-heir rather than by their worst moment.

children.heading: Old labels no longer name the whole story
bullets: Adulterer, drunk, liar, addict, hypocrite, failure, divorced, abandoned, damaged, and dirty may describe a chapter but do not name the book of a person washed by Jesus.
Paul’s “such were some of you” is followed by washed, sanctified, and justified in the Lord Jesus’ name.
Grace does not deny the old life; it makes that life no longer the truest fact about the believer.

children.heading: The blood, not shame or the past, names the cleansed person
bullets: Hearers are told to stop letting the accuser introduce them and to reject the names supplied by shame, failure, the past, or their own former self-description.
They are named washed, forgiven, justified, clean, and white as snow by Jesus’ blood.
Isaiah’s scarlet-to-snow promise is joined to David’s faith and to Jesus’ completed work at Calvary, sealed in the sermon’s image by hyssop touching Jesus’ lips.

movements.heading: Grace restores joy while discipline rescues
bullets: Grace is pictured as a wave that takes guilt away while bringing joy.
Psalm 51:8 asks not for pain or consequences to vanish but for broken bones to rejoice.

children.heading: Grace brings an undeserved gift as it removes guilt
bullets: Josh calls grace a wave that always washes something up while washing something away.
Grace removes guilt and restores joy.

children.heading: Psalm 51:8 asks to hear joy and gladness
bullets: Josh reads David’s request to hear joy and gladness and for the bones God has broken to rejoice.
Sin promised pleasure but produced misery, so David reaches toward restored joy.

children.heading: David seeks help carrying memories of the harm he caused
bullets: Josh voices David asking to hear something other than the cries he caused and to see something other than the death order sent through Uriah to Joab.
The memory remains, but David asks God for help carrying it.
The accusing voice may pester people not only about deeds but even about sinful thoughts.

children.heading: Believers may ask God to restore peace and joy
bullets: David believes God can silence accusing noise and fill him with joy, and Josh tells believers they can pray the same way and ask for peace.
Sin kills joy and overpromises while underdelivering; Bathsheba’s promised happiness yielded adultery, anxiety, fear, lies, manipulation, murder, silence, depression, and a dead child.

children.heading: Psalm 32 and Psalm 51 connect wasted and rejoicing bones
bullets: Psalm 32 says David’s bones wasted away while he kept silent; Psalm 51 asks that the bones God broke rejoice.
Josh states twice that God wounded David to rescue David.
Cultural praise for military toughness and hardship is contrasted with discomfort at the biblical claim that God disciplines those he loves.

children.heading: A loving Father intervenes against self-destruction
bullets: A loving God comforts people in pain but does not watch passively while his children destroy themselves.
As a good Father, he steps in even when his children do not want the intervention.

children.heading: Pray for rejoicing through pain, not merely removed consequences
bullets: Those who need joy are told to pray during the week for renewed joy and gladness.
David does not ask for consequences or even brokenness to be removed; he asks for joy and gladness through the pain.
The image concludes with broken bones learning to dance.

movements.heading: What David cannot hide, God can blot out
bullets: Psalm 51:9 reverses David’s failed concealment: unable to hide sin from God, David asks God to hide his face from it.
Confession receives mercy because Christ cancels the condemning record at the cross.

children.heading: David asks God to hide his face and blot out sin
bullets: Josh reads the request for God to hide his face from David’s sins and blot out all his iniquities.
For more than a year David tried and failed to hide sin from God; now he asks God to hide it from himself.
David’s attempted covering failed, while God’s covering works.

children.heading: God exposes concealment and covers confession
bullets: The sermon states the wisdom as a contrast: what people conceal, God exposes in love; what they confess, God covers in love.

children.heading: Proverbs locates mercy at confession and renunciation
bullets: Josh announces “Proverbs 28:3,” but the words he reads are Proverbs 28:13–14.
Those who conceal sins do not prosper; those who confess and renounce them find mercy.
The reading continues that those who tremble before God are blessed, while hard hearts fall into trouble.

children.heading: Blotting is pictured as annihilating the legal record
bullets: Josh notes that Psalm 51:1 and 51:9 both use “blot,” which he says can be rendered “annihilate,” and describes David as wanting the record gone.
Colossians 2 is read: God makes the dead alive with Christ, forgives sins, cancels the legal indebtedness that condemned them, takes it away, and nails it to the cross.

children.heading: Jesus’ finished work answers David’s prayer
bullets: David’s prayer is paraphrased as “Annihilate my sin record.”
Jesus’ last-breath declaration from the cross is invoked as finished, done, dead, dealt with, and paid.

movements.heading: God supplies in Christ what he delights in
bullets: The standards of inward truth, wisdom, purity, and righteousness expose what sinners cannot produce.
Psalm 51 restores hope because God produces what he delights in through his Son.

children.heading: God’s desires expose human inability
bullets: People lack the inward truth God delights in and cannot manufacture secret-heart wisdom.
They cannot cleanse themselves into the purity God requires and stand guilty before his demand for righteousness.
These requirements appear hopeless until Psalm 51 shows that God produces what he delights in.

children.heading: Christianity presents God’s standard and God’s Son
bullets: The message is not “Here is God’s standard; try harder,” but “Here is God’s standard, and here is God’s Son.”

children.heading: Jesus embodies everything Psalm 51 says God desires
bullets: Jesus is named as truth, perfect wisdom, perfect purity, and perfect obedience, without hypocrisy, deceit, hiding, pride, or selfishness.
From birth Jesus is everything in which God delighted, while human beings are sinners from birth.

children.heading: The great exchange gives peace with God
bullets: The perfect God-man takes shame, guilt, sin, debt, past, and crimes upon himself and gives peace with God in exchange.
David prays for what Jesus provides.

children.heading: God’s hiding and blotting prevent judgment from falling on the sinner
bullets: Josh says that if God does not hide his face from sin, he must hide his face from the sinner; if he does not annihilate sins, he must annihilate sinners.
The congregation praises God for making a way and confesses peace with God through the Lord Jesus Christ.

children.heading: The risen Christ reigns and will return
bullets: The Savior is not on the cross or in the tomb: the stone is rolled away, death defeated, the grave conquered, and Jesus alive.
Josh quotes the taunt asking death where its sting and victory are.
Jesus is described as ascended, seated at the Father’s right hand, ruling, reigning, and interceding, and as the king who will come again.
Josh anticipates dancing when he reaches God’s holy mountain and sees the King.

children.heading: Closing calls to ask boldly for inward renewal
bullets: Until Christ returns, believers are called to ask him to teach, purge, wash, restore joy amid chaos, and hide his face from remembered sin.
The week’s bold prayer is for God to annihilate anything within that he does not delight in, prayed with readiness to release it.
The next sermon will continue David’s requests to create, restore, and uphold.
Hearers are urged to ask God to go as deep as needed, make them clean and new in the secret heart, and renew them.

children.heading: Final prayer for cleansing and confident freedom
bullets: Josh prays as one who knows both hiding and crying out, especially for those afraid of what is truly inside them or unable to look at themselves.
He asks the Spirit to flood them with the truth that God can wash it away so they may walk under salvation in freedom and confidence, saying “I shall be clean.”

As the congregation smells, holds, and sees hyssop, sings, and comes around the table, he asks that the Old-to-New-Testament cleansing connection minister to them and remind them what Christ has done.
The prayer closes by asking that they call on God in need and walk with him every day.

ledger.phrase: Everyone ought to examine themselves before they eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
He did not come to be served, but to serve.
That’s why we shouldn’t forsake it. … We need to come in person.
Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart.
Verses 1–5 have been all about confession.
Nathan confronted David’s adultery, his murder.
The things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and these defile you.
The faith that was in Timothy actually lived in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice first.
Timothy had known the sacred Scriptures from childhood, Scriptures capable of making him wise for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ.
Who may dwell in your sanctuary? Who may live on your holy mountain?
Go read 2 Samuel chapter 11. David sees Bathsheba. He wants her. She becomes pregnant.
The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him.
The demons know the truth, and they tremble.
For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is what? … Eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
I am the vine, you are the branches. If you remain in me and I in you, you will bear much fruit.
If everything Jesus did were written down … the world itself could not … contain all the books.
You are a letter from Christ, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God.
You shall not commit adultery. You shall not murder. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean. Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
In Exodus 12, hyssop carries the Passover blood to the doorposts.
In Leviticus 14, hyssop was used by the priest to sprinkle the leper being cleansed.
The priest threw cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet wool into the fire.
A jar of wine vinegar was there. So they soaked a sponge in it, put the sponge on a stalk of the hyssop plant.
The blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin.
Such were some of you. … But you were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.
Let me hear joy and gladness. Let the bones that you have broken rejoice.
When I kept silent … my bones wasted away.
God disciplines those he loves.
Hide your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities.
Those who conceal their sins do not prosper, but those who confess and renounce them find mercy.
ledger.reference_note: Spoken as “Proverbs 28:3”; the quoted wording is Proverbs 28:13–14.

ledger.phrase: He forgave us all our sins, having cancelled the charge of our legal indebtedness which stood against us and condemned us.
We have peace with God through our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
Where, O death, is your sting? Where is your victory?
He is seated at the right hand of the Father. He is ruling over every power.
He is seated at the right hand of the Father … interceding for his people.
Create in me. Restore me. Uphold me.
